snippet.title: Why You Can't Stand On Jupiter
snippet.description:
What would you see if you fell into Jupiter? The colour is a cloud deck, not a surface. This film goes down through the bands, the 1995 Galileo probe, the last of the light, and a metal dark with no floor.

Chapters
0:00 The fall
0:37 The Cloud Deck
1:56 Nothing to Stand On
3:21 What the Probe Saw
4:53 The Last of the Light
6:25 The Metal Dark
8:25 What Else Has No Floor?

NASA’s Galileo probe went in on 7 December 1995. It lasted about 58 minutes, reached about 22 times the pressure of Earth’s air, and never found a surface. Juno’s gravity measurements point to a dilute core, not a hard marble in the middle.

Sources: Wahl et al. 2017, Geophysical Research Letters (Juno's gravity data and the dilute core); Sromovsky et al. 1996, Science (Galileo probe, sunlight under the clouds); Fortney & Nettelmann 2010, Space Science Reviews (megabar pressures inside giant planets); NASA Science, Galileo Jupiter Atmospheric Probe (entry on 7 Dec 1995, 58 minutes, 22.7 atmospheres); NASA Science, Jupiter Facts (10-hour day, three cloud layers, metallic hydrogen).

A new film on Sundays. What do you think you would still see once the light goes?

snippet.title: What Happens If You Fall Into a Black Hole?
snippet.description:
What happens if you fall into a black hole? Join Orbit — a small orange exploration robot — on a black holes explained cosmic journey across the event horizon. In this space documentary we explore spaghettification, time dilation, the singularity, Hawking radiation, and what scientists still don't know about falling into a black hole.

🌌 Chapters:

Find out what happens inside a black hole if you were pulled in. We break down the physics of black holes and the fate of travellers.

This journey explores the extreme conditions awaiting anyone crossing the event horizon. We examine the reality of spaghettification and how gravitational forces would alter your physical form. If you have ever questioned the physics of black holes, this visual guide provides a clear look at these cosmic phenomena.

We also investigate the effects of time dilation black hole theories suggest, explaining how time itself behaves near such massive density. By the end of this video, you will understand exactly what happens inside a black hole, from the initial approach to the singular point, without the dry academic lecture.

snippet.title: How Long Do Saturn's Rings Have Left?
snippet.description:
Saturn is losing its rings. The ice rings are raining away into the planet right now.

Saturn's rings are not a solid disc. They are water ice, chunks from grains to boulders, in a sheet only about ten metres thick. Astronomers using the Keck telescope measured ring rain falling into this gas giant along its magnetic field. Cassini's Grand Finale dives found a heavier leak from the D ring into Saturn's equator. Put together, the rings have somewhere between about 100 and 300 million years left. They won't last forever.

snippet.title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning?
snippet.description:
Right now, in Britain, the ground is carrying you east at about a thousand kilometres an hour, and you feel nothing. What if Earth stopped spinning? A sudden stop is a thought experiment: the air would keep going. The real story is that Earth is already slowing down, and the clocks have been keeping score.

The speed you cannot feel, then what a sudden stop would do to the air, what a slow stop would do to the seas and the length of a day, and how the Moon is already braking the spin. Fossil corals, ancient eclipses and leap seconds are how we know the day has been changing.

0:00 What If Earth Stopped Spinning?
0:23 The Sudden Stop
1:33 The Speed You Cannot Feel
2:55 A Slow Stop
4:08 Earth Is Already Slowing
5:56 Keeping Score

Sources: NASA GSFC Earth Fact Sheet (Williams), equatorial radius 6,378 km and a sidereal day of 23.93 hours, so the equator moves at about 1,670 km/h · NGA WGS 84, Earth is about 43 km wider across the equator than pole to pole · Stephenson, Morrison and Hohenkerk 2016 (Proceedings of the Royal Society A), the day lengthens by about 1.8 milliseconds a century · Wells 1963 (Nature), Middle Devonian corals show about 400 daily growth lines a year · Dickey et al. 1994 (Science), the Moon recedes by about 3.8 cm a year · IERS Bulletin C and NIST, 27 leap seconds from 1972 to 31 December 2016.

Images and footage courtesy of NASA (DSCOVR/EPIC, GSFC, ISS, Apollo, Armstrong) and NASA/JPL (PIA00271, PIA22223, PIA22929, PIA23791, PIA24573; Bennu journey plate is an artist's impression). Also ESA (Alexander Gerst ISS timelapses), ESO (Paranal star trails, La Silla timelapse), NOAA (2024 eclipse) and NIST (atomic clocks). Other plates: a Metropolitan Museum of Art cuneiform tablet, a Foucault pendulum, a portrait of Léon Foucault, fossil corals, the Bay of Fundy, and pāhoehoe lava.

snippet.description:
How Long Do Saturn's Rings Have Left?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=55AEQwvs36g

Saturn's main rings span tens of thousands of kilometres across, yet in places they are only about ten metres thick — ten times thinner than a 100-metre playing field. Drop through those ten metres and you are in open space again.

Sources: NASA, Saturn Fact Sheet / Cassini Solstice Mission (main rings ~10 metres thick in places); Iess et al. 2019, Science (Cassini Grand Finale ring mass and structure).

Pictures: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute Cassini imagery (PIA18367, PIA21057, PIA09805, PIA06092, PIA08992, PIA07872, PIA21886) alongside AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.

snippet.title: Why Haven't We Found Aliens Yet? The Fermi Paradox Explained
snippet.description:
Are we alone in the universe? The Fermi Paradox explained — if the Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars and countless planets, why does the sky stay so quiet?

In this Orbit's Cosmic Journey film, Orbit explores the Fermi Paradox, the Great Filter, the zoo hypothesis, the limits of interstellar communication, and how humanity might detect alien life. The first convincing sign may not be a spacecraft or a dramatic message. It may be a faint chemical fingerprint, an unusual pulse, or a clue already hidden inside old data.

CHAPTERS

The Fermi paradox asks why we have not encountered alien civilizations yet. Explore the vastness of space and the odds of life existing elsewhere.

This exploration examines the scale of the universe, from Earth's signal transmissions to the observation of distant galaxies. It breaks down the statistical likelihood of life on other planets and analyses why humanity has not made contact with extraterrestrial life despite the age of the universe.

Whether you are interested in astronomy or the search for life beyond Earth, this overview provides context on the current scientific perspective regarding the Fermi paradox. It details how signals travel through space and what we know about the potential for other civilisations among the stars.

snippet.title: What Happened to Venus?
snippet.description:
Venus is Earth's twin: almost the same size, made of the same rock, and it even soaks up less sunlight than Earth does. Yet its surface is hot enough to melt lead. So what happened to Venus?

Its air is about 96% carbon dioxide, ninety times thicker than ours, and the heat cannot get out: a runaway greenhouse. Earth holds about as much carbon dioxide, locked away in limestone and seabed by water. Venus has lost its water. Pioneer Venus found its heavy hydrogen (deuterium) about a hundred times richer than Earth's, the fingerprint of water broken apart and leaked to space. Whether Venus ever had oceans is still open: one climate model says shallow seas for billions of years, another says the steam never came down. DAVINCI, VERITAS and EnVision are designed to go back and read the rocks.

snippet.description:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

snippet.title: How Far Is the Nearest Star?
snippet.description:
How far is the nearest star? Proxima Centauri, a small red dwarf 4.24 light-years away, is so faint you can never see it without a telescope. Even light, the fastest thing there is, takes more than four years to cross the gap.

We meet Proxima and its bright neighbours Alpha Centauri A and B, find out how parallax and the Gaia spacecraft measure a distance that large, from Friedrich Bessel's first star distance in 1838 to more than a billion stars today, and shrink the light-year down to a grapefruit Sun and a cherry-sized star thousands of kilometres away. Then the journey: how long it would take on foot, by car, by jet, at the speed of Voyager 1 and at the speed of light, and what waits at the end, the planet Proxima b and the Breakthrough Starshot plan to reach it.

snippet.title: What Happens When Gliese 710 Passes Through the Oort Cloud?

snippet.title: Is the Sun Getting Brighter?
snippet.description:
The Sun is getting brighter, about 1% every 110 million years. And it brightens because it is running out of fuel.

The Sun turns hydrogen into helium in its core. Helium packs more mass into fewer particles, so as the ash builds up the core loses pressure, squeezes in, heats up and fuses faster. More fusion means more light. That is why the young Sun was about 30% dimmer, why early Earth still had oceans (a thicker greenhouse made up the difference), and why, about a billion years from now, a Sun some 10% brighter starts to push Earth's oceans towards a moist greenhouse. Sunspots and prominences are a different clock: the 11-year cycle moves the total light by only about 0.1%, up and down.

Nothing you can see in the night sky is permanent — from Saturn's ice rings raining into the planet right now to the last red dwarf stars shining ten trillion years from now. How long does each of them have left?

snippet.title: What Happens If You Travel Near Light Speed?
snippet.description:
Leave Earth at ninety-nine percent of the speed of light for one year by your own watch, and seven years pass at home. What happens if you travel near the speed of light? That gap is time dilation, and special relativity says nobody cheated: a moving clock really runs slow.

Your phone already depends on it. GPS satellite clocks drift by about 38 millionths of a second a day, and left alone the map would wander by around ten kilometres a day. In 1971 atomic clocks flown around the world on airliners came home out of step, and muons from cosmic rays reach the ground only because their clocks run slow. We follow the twin paradox on a trip to a star ten light-years away, see why each extra nine of speed costs more energy than the last, and why a ship accelerating at one Earth gravity could cross the entire Milky Way within a single crew lifetime—at an irreversible cost to everyone left on Earth.

snippet.title: Why Will Gliese 710's Comets Arrive After It Has Gone?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

Gliese 710 is predicted to send about 10 extra comets a year into the inner Solar System for three to four million years — yet the comet shower peaks only after the star has already passed and is heading away again, because falling in from the distant Oort Cloud takes hundreds of thousands of years.

Sources: Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — predicted Oort Cloud comet flux (~10 observable comets/yr lasting 3–4 Myr) (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a) · NASA Science, Oort Cloud Facts — the distant comet reservoir (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/oort-cloud/facts/).
